claim: Pick a typeface category from the job the text does, not from taste: sans-serif for interface and screen copy, serif for long-form reading, display strictly for oversized headline elements.
why: Each category was shaped by a different constraint — screen rendering, sustained reading at small sizes, and single-glance impact — so category choice is a functional decision before it is an aesthetic one.
when: Choosing the typefaces for a new project or auditing an existing type stack.
fails: Editorial or print-flavoured products deliberately invert the convention, and high-DPI screens plus well-hinted screen serifs have narrowed the legibility gap enough that a serif UI can work when tested.

claim: Never set paragraph or UI-scale text in a display or handwritten face; cap those to headline, hero, and logotype sizes where the ornamentation is still resolvable.
why: Display faces carry detail sized for large rendering; below roughly headline scale that detail collapses into visual noise and letterforms stop being distinguishable at a glance.
when: Any layout where a decorative face is being considered for more than a few words.

claim: When a design needs to read as established, traditional, or authoritative, reach for a serif; when it needs to read as current, neutral, or utilitarian, reach for a sans-serif.
why: Serifs carry centuries of association with printed books and institutions, while sans-serifs are read as contemporary because that is what today's dominant interfaces use — readers decode the tone before they read a word.
when: Brand and product work where the type has to signal a position (finance, law, publishing vs. software, startups, consumer apps).
fails: The association is cultural and audience-dependent, not intrinsic; a geometric sans can feel institutional and a modern serif can feel fashion-forward, so treat it as a starting bias to test rather than a rule.

claim: Test any serif you intend to use for body copy at its smallest real size before committing, since the serif's legibility advantage depends on the stroke details actually surviving rendering.
why: The claimed small-size legibility benefit comes from the terminal strokes helping the eye differentiate and track letterforms — if those strokes are too fine to render, the benefit disappears and the face becomes worse than a sans.
when: Setting extended body text, captions, or dense tabular data in a serif.

claim: Treat handwritten faces as display faces with the same size floor, and vet them for how convincingly they simulate written text before use.
why: They are a decorative subgroup, and quality varies widely — many read as an imitation of handwriting rather than as handwriting, which undercuts the warmth they were chosen for.
when: Adding a personal, informal, or signature-like accent to a layout.

claim: Measure x-height off a flat-topped, flat-bottomed lowercase letter such as 'x', not off a round letter like 'e', 'o', or 's'.
why: Curved and pointed glyphs are drawn with a slight optical overshoot — they extend a hair past the reference line so they don't read as smaller than their flat neighbours — so measuring from them gives a value a fraction too large.
when: Taking measurements from a typeface, comparing x-heights across candidate fonts, or building a vertical rhythm/optical-alignment spec from real glyph metrics.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter; note that this is a measurement convention, not a rendering rule — layout engines still position round glyphs with their overshoot intact, so you cannot cancel overshoot by nudging individual letters.

claim: Measure cap height off a flat-bottomed, flat-topped capital such as 'E', 'H', or 'T', for the same overshoot reason.
why: Capitals like 'O', 'C' and 'S' also overshoot both the baseline and the cap line; only flat-terminated capitals sit exactly on the two reference lines.
when: Reading cap height from a specimen, or setting optical top/bottom padding on a button or badge where the label is all-caps.

claim: Reason about vertical type placement using three reference lines — baseline, x-height, cap height — rather than the font's bounding box.
why: The bounding box includes ascender, descender and internal leading space that varies wildly between typefaces; the three anatomical lines describe where the ink actually is, which is what the eye aligns to.
when: Aligning text with icons, avatars or adjacent text of a different size; setting up a vertical rhythm; deciding what 'centred' means inside a container.
fails: CSS and most layout tools position by line box, not by cap height — so achieving cap-height alignment requires deliberate offsets or a trim/leading-trim utility rather than default centring.

claim: Scale letter spacing inversely with font size: add positive tracking as text gets smaller, and apply negative tracking as text gets larger.
why: Letter spacing that looks correct at one size is proportionally too tight or too loose at another — large type carries enough visual mass that default gaps read as gaps, while small type needs extra breathing room for the letterforms to stay distinguishable.
when: Setting a type scale where display headings and caption/label text both use the same family; any time one tracking value is being reused across sizes.
fails: Not addressed here; in practice good text faces already ship optical sizing or size-appropriate defaults at body sizes, so tracking adjustments belong at the extremes of the scale, not on every step.

claim: When learning a technical vocabulary for practical use, extract only the terms that change decisions, and skip the rest.
why: Full font anatomy runs to dozens of terms (aperture, spur, terminal, shoulder...), almost none of which a screen designer will ever adjust; the three vertical metrics and tracking are the ones that show up in real layout decisions.
when: Building working knowledge of a craft discipline under time pressure.
fails: Type designers, font engineers and anyone doing hinting or variable-font work need the full vocabulary.

claim: Build and reuse a small personal font library — three or four typefaces you know well can carry the overwhelming majority of your projects; treat re-picking fonts from scratch each time as the exception, not the default.
why: Open-ended browsing of huge font libraries burns hours and usually ends in a fatigued default choice rather than a considered one; a known, trusted set removes the search cost and gives predictable results.
when: General project work where typography is a supporting decision rather than the brand differentiator itself, and you're choosing type under time pressure.
fails: Brand identity work or projects whose whole point is a distinctive typographic voice — there, defaulting to your usual set produces work that looks like everything else you've made.

claim: Constrain your font search to a single trusted free source (e.g. Google Fonts) and check licensing for the intended use before committing — free for personal use does not mean free for commercial use.
why: A bounded, license-clear source makes the shortlist small enough to actually decide from, and catches the licensing problem before the typeface is embedded in delivered work.
when: Selecting typefaces for web work where budget rules out licensed foundry fonts.
fails: Client or commercial work where the personal-use license doesn't cover distribution, or where the brand requires a typeface not available on free platforms.

claim: Avoid Comic Sans in professional design work regardless of whether you can articulate a technical objection to it.
why: The typeface carries such strong negative professional connotation that using it signals amateurism to the audience whose opinion matters, independent of its letterform quality.
when: Any professional or portfolio design context.
fails: Deliberately playful, ironic, or children's contexts, and accessibility cases where its irregular letterforms genuinely aid some dyslexic readers — the chapter treats the rule as a joke and does not address these.

claim: Cap a site at two typefaces by default; treat three as an exception that requires each face to own a distinct, non-overlapping role, and never ship four.
why: Each additional typeface adds a visual voice the reader has to learn; past two, the page stops reading as one system and starts reading as inconsistency. A single-font site is not a limitation — plenty of high-quality production sites do it.
when: Choosing the type stack for any marketing, portfolio, or product site.
fails: Not addressed for the upper bound; the speaker states they've seen no good four-font site rather than proving one can't exist.

claim: When a site uses only one typeface, pick a sans-serif.
why: Sans-serifs are the neutral default for screen reading and carry no strong period signal, so a single face can cover every role without the whole site inheriting a specific era or genre.
when: Single-typeface sites with no deliberate historical or thematic voice.
fails: When the brand is intentionally period-styled — medieval, antique, editorial-historical — in which case the atypical face is the point.

claim: For a two-font pairing, use one of two proven combinations: display + sans-serif, or sans-serif + serif.
why: Both pairings put maximum contrast at the level of role rather than at the level of similarity — the two faces are obviously different, so the reader reads hierarchy instead of noticing a near-miss mismatch.
when: Any two-typeface web design.
fails: Pairing two faces from the same category (two sans-serifs, two serifs), where the difference is too small to read as intentional.

claim: A handwritten or script face is a valid drop-in replacement for the display face in a display + sans pairing.
why: Its job in the pairing is identical to the display face's — carry personality at large sizes — so it slots into the same role without changing the structure of the pairing.
when: Sites wanting a warmer or more personal voice in headlines than a geometric display face provides.
fails: Anywhere the face would be asked to do body-text work.

claim: Never set small paragraph text in a display or handwritten typeface; restrict those faces to headlines and other large sizes.
why: Display and script faces are drawn for impact at large sizes — their letterforms lose legibility and their quirks compound when scaled down to reading size.
when: All body copy, running text, and any type set at reading size.
fails: Not addressed — the rule is stated as absolute.

claim: If you go to three typefaces, justify it by assigning each face a role no other face touches: display for headlines, sans-serif for body and UI, and a third distinctive face reserved for small metadata such as captions and image credits.
why: Three faces only stay coherent if the reader can infer why each one appears — role separation makes the third face read as a labelling system rather than as clutter.
when: Portfolio and expressive sites where a small, contained category of text (captions, credits, technical detail) genuinely differs in kind from body copy.
fails: When the third face bleeds into body copy or duplicates a role the other two already cover.

claim: Monospace works well as the third face for captions and micro-detail text.
why: Its mechanical, evenly-spaced rhythm reads as annotation or technical labelling — visibly a different class of text from the prose — while still being legible at small sizes, which display and script faces are not.
when: Three-font systems needing a visual marker for captions, credits, or metadata.
fails: As a body-text face, where the uniform character widths slow sustained reading.

claim: Treat font weight and text colour as one perceptual control — apparent ink density — and pick either one, or both, to separate a primary from a secondary text level.
why: At typical body sizes, reducing weight and reducing opacity both shrink the amount of dark pixel area a glyph puts on screen, and the eye reads that area as 'lightness' regardless of which property caused it.
when: Establishing hierarchy between text elements in a layout — headings vs. body, label vs. value, primary vs. supporting copy.
fails: At large display sizes, where the stroke shape is legible enough that a thin heavy-coloured headline and a bold faded one no longer look alike; the two levers separate again.

claim: Build a text hierarchy using colour alone, or weight alone — you do not need to vary both to make levels distinguishable.
why: Since both properties move the same perceptual dimension, one is sufficient; using only one keeps the type system simpler and more predictable.
when: Designing a layout with two or three text levels where you want a minimal, consistent set of type styles.
fails: When the levels also need to differ in role, not just in prominence (e.g. an interactive link vs. static text), where a single dimension of contrast may not carry the meaning.

claim: For regular running text, choose weights from the middle of the family and avoid the extreme ends — skip ultra-thin/hairline and ultra-bold/black cuts.
why: Extreme weights compromise legibility at text sizes: hairlines lose stroke definition and blacks close up counters, and neither behaves reliably across rendering environments.
when: Setting body copy, labels, captions, and other text meant to be read rather than looked at.
fails: Large display type and single-word logotypes, where extreme cuts are used deliberately as a visual gesture and legibility risk is low.

claim: Set primary text at full opacity and secondary text somewhere in the 40–70% opacity band of the same colour, rather than picking unrelated grey values.
why: Deriving the secondary tone from the primary keeps the palette coherent, and that band is far enough down to read as demoted but still comfortably readable.
when: Assigning colour to a two-tier text hierarchy on a solid background.
fails: Low-contrast backgrounds, over imagery, or where a WCAG contrast minimum applies — a 40% tone can fall below the required ratio and must be checked, not assumed.

claim: Whichever lever you use, make each step large enough to be unmistakable — verify the levels look different, don't just verify the numbers differ.
why: A hierarchy that is technically present but perceptually invisible does no work; near-neighbour weights or opacities read as an inconsistency rather than an intentional level.
when: Any time you assign more than one weight or text colour within the same layout.

claim: When you already vary weight between two text levels, don't stack a large opacity drop on top of it — the two reductions compound into a step bigger than intended.
why: Both changes subtract from the same pool of apparent ink, so their effects add rather than acting as independent signals.
when: Combining weight and colour on the same pair of text elements.
fails: When you genuinely want a very strong separation, such as fine print against a bold heading.

claim: Write down the ordered hierarchy of every text role before assigning its font styles.
why: Styling decisions should express each element’s communicative rank rather than be applied element by element without a system.
when: Designing or revising any interface with more than one kind of text.

claim: Do not automatically stack every emphasis treatment on headings; a sufficiently large heading can lead the hierarchy without also being bold or given special opacity.
why: Font size alone can establish strong visual priority, leaving other attributes available for other text roles.
when: A heading is materially larger than the surrounding text and must be the primary focal point.
fails: When size cannot create enough distinction because of tight space, similar scales, or accessibility constraints.

claim: Keep paragraph copy at full opacity instead of making the smallest text the faintest text.
why: Low contrast on the text users need to read most continuously harms usability and can look weak.
when: Styling normal body copy in reading-heavy UI content.

claim: Make subheadings more scannable than body copy by increasing their weight.
why: Section labels need to stand out during quick scanning while body copy remains readable at normal weight.
when: Subheadings divide or label groups of paragraphs or content blocks.

claim: Treat font size as responsive while keeping the overall hierarchy system and core choices such as colours, weights, and pairings consistent across screens.
why: Screen dimensions change the available space and therefore the appropriate text scale.
when: Adapting a UI typography system across viewport sizes.

claim: Generate every font size in a style guide by repeatedly multiplying a single base size by one fixed ratio, rather than picking each size by eye on a representative page.
why: A constant multiplier guarantees the size relationships stay consistent across pages you haven't designed yet; eyeballed sizes only encode what looked right in one specific composition.
when: Building a type scale intended to serve an entire product or site, not a one-off page.
fails: Not addressed directly, though the chapter concedes the eyeball method 'is not wrong' — for a single fixed layout the systematic scale buys little.

claim: Anchor the scale to a 16px base for body text and generate headings upward from it.
why: It is the browser default body size and gives the scale a concrete, readable starting point that every other step is expressed relative to.
when: Web layouts where paragraph text is the dominant content.

claim: Use a ratio of roughly 1.62 (the golden ratio) only when you need one or two size steps — for example a single heading sitting above body copy.
why: At two steps the jump reads as a confident, well-proportioned contrast; the ratio's problems only surface when compounded.
when: Simple content pages with a headline and paragraph text and little else.
fails: The moment the system needs four or more steps, since compounding 1.62 explodes the top end.

claim: Before adopting a ratio, compound it out to your largest heading and check the result — 16px scaled by 1.62 four times lands near 110px, which is too large for most interfaces.
why: Ratios behave innocently at one step and exponentially at four; the only way to catch the blow-up is to actually compute the top of the scale.
when: Any time you choose a modular scale ratio for a multi-level heading hierarchy.
fails: Editorial or poster-like layouts where a 110px display heading is the intended effect.

claim: When you need more steps than a large ratio allows, take a root of it instead of inventing a new number: the square root of the golden ratio (~1.27) is the general-purpose scaling factor.
why: Rooting preserves the original proportional relationship — two 1.27 steps still equal one golden-ratio step — so intermediate sizes like subheadings fall naturally between the sizes you already had.
when: Typical marketing sites and product pages with four to six type sizes.

claim: Drop to the cube root of the golden ratio (~1.17) for dense interfaces such as dashboards, or for mobile layouts where vertical space is scarce.
why: Dense UIs need many distinguishable text roles packed into a small range, and constrained viewports can't accommodate large headings; a tighter multiplier delivers more usable steps per unit of size.
when: Admin panels, data-heavy tools, mobile breakpoints, or any design system carrying a large inventory of text styles.
fails: Steps this close together risk becoming visually indistinguishable, so hierarchy has to be carried by weight or colour as well as size — the chapter doesn't raise this.

claim: Pick the ratio from how many distinct text roles your design needs — more roles demand a smaller multiplier.
why: Step count and ratio size trade off against each other; the total range from smallest to largest is the ratio raised to the number of steps, so the two can't be chosen independently.
when: At the point of defining a type scale, before any sizes are committed.

claim: Validate a new type scale by applying it to a real design and toggling between the old and new versions rather than judging the numbers in isolation.
why: The improvement from a well-proportioned scale is subtle and only legible in comparison; a list of pixel values gives no signal about whether the composition improved.
when: Retrofitting a systematic scale onto an existing design.

claim: Expect a scale change to be a refinement, not a redesign — accept a subtle improvement as a success rather than pushing the ratio until the change looks dramatic.
why: The narrator explicitly characterises the result as 'not a massive change' yet still worth doing, setting the correct expectation for the payoff.
when: Introducing a modular scale into work that already looks broadly acceptable.

claim: Compute font size as a continuous function of viewport width — smallestSize + (largestSize − smallestSize) × ((currentWidth − smallestWidth) / (largestWidth − smallestWidth)) — rather than redeclaring sizes inside media queries.
why: Interpolation gives a correct size at every width, not just at the handful of widths you thought to write rules for, and it collapses many per-breakpoint declarations into one expression per size.
when: Body and heading sizes in a type scale that should feel proportionate on any device.
fails: Sizes that must snap to a specific value at a specific width — a logo lockup, a fixed-height UI chrome element, or a design where mobile deliberately uses a different hierarchy rather than a shrunken one — still need explicit breakpoint overrides.

claim: Anchor the interpolation to a defined smallest and largest viewport width — 320px and 1920px are sane defaults — and define the type scale only at those two endpoints.
why: The ratio term needs a fixed domain to normalise against; picking the narrowest phone and a common large desktop covers the realistic range, and everything between is derived rather than decided.
when: Setting up a fluid scale for a general-audience responsive site.
fails: Audience data says otherwise — a design targeting ultrawide dashboards or small embedded displays should move the anchors to match its real width distribution.

claim: Design the type scale by specifying only two states: the size on the smallest screen and the size on the largest. Do not hand-author intermediate sizes.
why: Every intermediate value is a linear consequence of the two endpoints, so authoring them by hand only creates opportunities for the scale to drift out of proportion.
when: Any fluid-type setup.

claim: Always clamp a fluid size: wrap the interpolation so that max() holds it above the mobile size and min() holds it below the desktop size.
why: The interpolation is a line, not a segment — it keeps extrapolating outside the anchor widths, so an unusually wide monitor produces text larger than anything you designed and a narrow one produces text smaller.
when: Any time the formula is deployed to real users, whose viewport widths you do not control.
fails: If oversized text on ultrawide screens genuinely suits the design, the upper bound can be dropped deliberately — but that should be a decision, not an oversight.

claim: Use max() for the lower bound and min() for the upper bound: max(floorSize, formula) pulls an undersized result back up, min(ceilingSize, formula) pulls an oversized result back down.
why: The functions are counterintuitive by name — max enforces a minimum because it picks whichever value is larger, so the floor wins when the formula falls below it.
when: Hand-writing bounded fluid values in CSS.

claim: Verify a fluid sizing formula by plotting it as size-versus-width before shipping it, not by resizing a browser window.
why: The graph makes the out-of-range extrapolation obvious at a glance; window-dragging only ever samples widths inside the range you happen to test.
when: Introducing any viewport-derived calculation — type, spacing, or container sizing.

claim: Hand designs off as a mobile spec and a desktop spec with the promise that everything between interpolates, instead of specifying breakpoint behaviour designers won't define.
why: Breakpoints are an implementation artifact; designers typically deliver two or three fixed-width artboards and leave the in-between undefined, so a continuous system removes the ambiguity rather than papering over it.
when: Design-to-development handoff on responsive web work.

claim: Set body/paragraph line-height to approximately 150% of the font size (1.5 unitless).
why: At paragraph sizes the eye needs a clear horizontal channel to track from the end of one line back to the start of the next; too-tight leading causes line doubling and skipping.
when: Running body copy at typical reading sizes (roughly 14-20px) in a normal-width text column.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter, though it is presented as a rule of thumb rather than an absolute — very narrow columns or very short text blocks will want less.

claim: Set heading line-height to approximately 110-130% of the font size, tightening toward 110% as the heading gets larger.
why: Large type already creates generous optical space between lines; default leading leaves headings looking disconnected and airy, so they stop reading as a single unit.
when: Display and heading type that wraps to two or more lines.
fails: Single-line headings, where leading has no visible effect; also descender/ascender collision becomes a risk if you push below ~100%.

claim: Treat line-height as inversely proportional to font size: as size goes up, reduce the multiplier; as size goes down, increase it.
why: Leading is about the ratio of white space to letterform mass, not an absolute distance. A fixed multiplier applied across a whole type scale over-spaces the top end and under-spaces the bottom.
when: Defining line-height tokens across an entire type scale rather than for a single size.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: Increase line-height when the measure (line length) is longer, and reduce it when the column is narrow.
why: Longer lines make the return sweep to the next line harder to land accurately; extra leading gives the eye a wider target and lowers the chance of re-reading the same line.
when: Wide single-column text, full-bleed content blocks, or any layout where the measure exceeds a comfortable character count.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: Override the browser's or tool's automatic line-height explicitly for large display type instead of leaving it on the default.
why: Auto leading is calibrated for body-size text and produces proportionally too much space once type gets large, so the flaw only becomes visible at the top of the scale.
when: Hero headlines, section titles, and any type set well above body size.
fails: Everyday body and UI text, where the default is close enough that overriding it adds work without a visible payoff.

claim: Before shipping, review typography rendered at real size on the device class the design is actually for, rather than judging it from a zoomed canvas.
why: Perceived size, contrast, and legibility of type all shift with viewing distance and pixel density; a design that reads well on a zoomed desktop canvas can fail on a phone held at arm's length.
when: Final review of any layout before handoff or release.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: Express line-height as a ratio or percentage of font size rather than a fixed pixel value.
why: A ratio keeps the leading relationship intact automatically when the font size changes across breakpoints or scale steps; a pixel value silently breaks it.
when: Building responsive type systems or design tokens.
fails: Vertical-rhythm systems that deliberately snap every line to a fixed baseline grid, where an absolute value is the point.

claim: When a section's message is short and central, set it in a distinctive display typeface at large scale and let the type itself be the visual — do not pair it with decorative imagery it has to compete with.
why: A single strong typeface carries personality and hierarchy on its own; the chapter's whole premise is that expressive text reads as a designed element rather than as filler.
when: Hero sections, manifesto or statement blocks, section openers, and any moment where one sentence carries the weight of the screen.
fails: Long-form reading passages and UI labels, where a display face slows comprehension and should be swapped for a neutral text face.

claim: To source typography, reverse-engineer sites whose type you admire: open devtools, select the text node, and read the font family and font file URL from the sources/network panel instead of scrolling a font library hoping to recognise something.
why: You already know the face works in context because you have seen it working; browsing catalogues asks you to evaluate a typeface in isolation, which is slower and a worse predictor of fit.
when: Early in a project when you need a typographic direction fast and have reference sites you like.
fails: When the site uses a paid, self-hosted, or bespoke commissioned face — identification does not confer a right to use it.

claim: Before shipping any font lifted from another site, verify its licence covers your use — web embedding, self-hosting, and commercial projects are separately licensed — and buy or substitute a free lookalike if it does not.
why: Identifying a typeface and being permitted to redistribute it are different things; unlicensed font files in a production bundle are an actual legal exposure, not a style question.
when: Any time a font file or family name is taken from a third-party site into your own build.

claim: Vary the typographic treatment down a page rather than repeating one paragraph style — alternate scale, weight, and face so that key statements break out of the body rhythm.
why: Uniform stacked paragraphs give the reader no signal about what matters; contrast in type creates hierarchy and pacing without adding new elements.
when: Marketing pages, landing pages, and editorial layouts with mixed content.
fails: Dense documentation or data-heavy interfaces, where consistent type is what makes content scannable.

claim: Pair a distinctive typeface with an entrance animation on the text itself — animate the letters or lines in rather than fading in a container that happens to hold text.
why: Animating the type reinforces that the text is the subject of the section; the reveal draws attention to the words instead of to a surrounding box.
when: Above-the-fold statements and section headings that enter on scroll.
fails: When repeated on every heading, which turns the reveal into noise and delays reading.

claim: Choose the typeface first and derive the section's treatment from it, rather than picking a layout and dropping in whatever default font is available.
why: The demonstrated pattern is that the face carries the personality, and the animation and layout are built to showcase it — reversing the order leaves you decorating around a generic face.
when: Type-led sections where the copy is the primary content.
fails: Product UI built on an existing design system, where the type stack is fixed and layout leads instead.

claim: Ship an interface with a single typeface family; only add a second when a concrete need forces it, not by default.
why: Multiple families add coordination cost and visual noise without adding meaning; weight, size, and colour already generate enough differentiation for almost any interface.
when: General product UI, landing pages, dashboards — anywhere the goal is clarity rather than editorial expression.
fails: Brand systems built on an intentional serif/sans pairing, editorial and long-form reading contexts, or when a monospace face is needed for code and tabular figures.

claim: Default to a neutral, widely-used sans-serif (the Inter/Helvetica-adjacent class of grotesques) and treat the choice as settled rather than a design exercise.
why: Neutral grotesques are reliably legible at UI sizes and rarely the reason a design fails; time spent auditioning faces buys less than time spent on hierarchy and spacing.
when: Starting any new interface, especially under time pressure or without an existing brand system.
fails: The product's differentiation depends on typographic personality, or a client brand mandates a specific face.

claim: For display and headline text, tighten letter-spacing to roughly -2% to -3% of the font size and set line-height to about 110-120%.
why: Type is optically spaced for body sizes; scaled up, the same relative tracking and leading read as gaps, so headlines look loose and amateur until they are optically corrected.
when: Any text set noticeably larger than body copy — hero headlines, section titles, large numerals in stat blocks.
fails: Body and caption sizes, where negative tracking and sub-130% line-height hurt readability; also fails on already-tight faces or all-caps and small text, which usually need positive tracking.

claim: Treat tracking and line-height as functions of size: as type gets larger, both should get proportionally tighter.
why: The relationship is optical, not fixed — a single global line-height applied across a scale will leave headlines airy and body text cramped.
when: Defining a type scale where each step carries its own spacing values.
fails: Not addressed for the extreme small end, where the inverse (looser tracking) applies.

claim: Limit a marketing site or landing page to at most six distinct font sizes, spread across a wide range from small captions to large display.
why: A bounded set forces every size to carry a distinct hierarchical role; beyond that, sizes stop signalling level and start reading as inconsistency.
when: Landing pages, marketing sites, and other low-density persuasive layouts.
fails: Very large content systems or documentation with many nesting levels may legitimately need more steps.

claim: In dense product UI such as dashboards, compress the type scale hard and keep almost all text at or below roughly 24px.
why: High information density means many elements compete for the same screen; large type steals space and creates false emphasis where the data itself should be the focal point.
when: Admin panels, analytics dashboards, data tables, and other tool-like interfaces.
fails: A single hero metric or KPI intentionally set large as the screen's focal point, and mobile layouts where minimum legible sizes push the whole scale up.

claim: Pick the width of the type scale from the interface's information density before choosing individual sizes.
why: Density determines how much contrast between levels is affordable; the same six-step scale that works on a landing page will break a dashboard.
when: Setting up a type system at the start of a project, once the product type is known.
fails: Design systems spanning both marketing and product surfaces, which need two scales sharing one family rather than one compromise scale.

claim: Before designing a section, gather real shipped examples of that same section pattern from products with strong design teams.
why: Working from solved real-world cases beats inventing from scratch and shows conventions users already understand.
when: Starting a screen or being stuck on a specific component or section.
fails: Copying surface style without the underlying constraints; the reference product's context may not match yours.

claim: Differentiate text levels with three properties in combination — size, weight, and colour — rather than resolving all hierarchy through size alone.
why: Size is the most obvious signal, so designers stop there; layering weight and colour produces separation between levels without pushing type scales further apart.
when: Any text block with more than one level of importance: headings with subcopy, card titles with metadata, labels with values.

claim: Use at most two font weights in a single interface or composition.
why: Weight variety follows the same rule as size variety — past two steps, the extra distinctions stop reading as hierarchy and start reading as noise.
when: Choosing the type styles for a screen or component set.
fails: Large editorial or marketing systems may legitimately need a display weight in addition to the two UI weights; the cap is a working default, not a hard ceiling.

claim: When picking two weights from a large family, skip at least one intermediate weight between them (e.g. Regular and Semibold, not Regular and Medium).
why: Adjacent weights in a many-weight family are too similar to register as distinct at body sizes, so the contrast does no hierarchical work.
when: Working with variable fonts or families shipping many weight steps.

claim: Limit text colour to two values: one primary ink (black on light, white on dark) and a reduced-opacity version of that same ink for secondary text.
why: Deriving the secondary colour from the primary keeps it in the same hue family, so it reads as de-emphasis rather than as a second, competing colour.
when: Setting body, caption, metadata, and supporting copy in a UI.
fails: Semantic colours (error, success, links) fall outside this count and are chosen by meaning, not hierarchy.

claim: Set secondary text opacity between 45% and 70% of the primary ink, tuning within that band to the context.
why: Below the band the text loses legibility; above it the text no longer separates from the primary level.
when: Producing a de-emphasised text tier from a primary text colour.
fails: On low-contrast backgrounds or small type, 45% may drop below accessible contrast — the band assumes a strong base contrast to start from.

claim: Prefer opacity-derived secondary ink over hand-picking a separate grey.
why: A single opacity value stays correct across light and dark surfaces, whereas an independently chosen grey has to be re-picked per background.
when: Defining text colour tokens for a theme that inverts.

claim: When a layout feels flat, add weight and colour differentiation before restructuring the layout or altering spacing.
why: It is the cheapest intervention available — the composition, sizes, and structure stay put while the perceived quality jump is large.
when: Polishing a design that is structurally sound but reads as undifferentiated.
fails: If the underlying information architecture is wrong, styling contrast will not fix which content deserves prominence.

claim: When a section needs visual impact, consider setting a short line of copy at hero scale in a display typeface instead of reaching for an image or illustration.
why: A well-drawn display face carries enough character and visual mass to anchor a composition the way a photograph would, so it can fill the 'hero visual' slot without any asset production.
when: Hero sections, section openers, and any layout that needs a focal point but has no strong imagery available.
fails: The typeface is a neutral workhorse (a plain grotesque or system font) — scaling that up reads as an accident rather than a deliberate visual, so the substitution only works with a face that has distinct character.

claim: Limit oversized display type to one occurrence per page, and never more than two.
why: The effect works by contrast against normal-scale text; repeating it flattens the hierarchy so nothing reads as the focal point and the page reads as shouting.
when: Any single page or continuous scroll where large-scale type is being used for impact.
fails: Not addressed — no exception given for very long pages with distinct sections.

claim: Pick display typefaces deliberately from a curated shortlist rather than defaulting to whatever the body face offers at a large size.
why: Display faces are drawn for large sizes — their tight spacing and expressive letterforms only resolve at scale — so the choice of face is what makes giant type look intentional.
when: Choosing the typeface for the one or two headline moments in a layout.
fails: Using a display face for body copy or long-form reading, where its distinctive letterforms and tight fit hurt legibility.

claim: Source new display faces by filtering a free font library (e.g. Google Fonts) on the display category and browsing the results, rather than searching by name.
why: The category filter turns typeface discovery into a repeatable browsing task instead of relying on recall of font names you already know.
when: Building or refreshing a personal shortlist of headline typefaces for a project.

claim: Keep the giant-type line short enough to hold as a shape — it must still read as language, not just decoration.
why: The copy is doing double duty: it is the visual anchor and it still has to explain the page, so it cannot be sacrificed to the composition.
when: Writing and setting the headline that will carry the display treatment.
fails: Long sentences or paragraphs set at display scale, where the type stops functioning as a single visual mass and becomes hard to read.

claim: Apply negative letter-spacing of roughly -2% to -4% of the font size to any text set above ~70-80px.
why: Typefaces are spaced for reading sizes; that same relative spacing scales up proportionally and reads as gaps between letters at display size.
when: Hero headlines, display type, oversized section headers, landing-page statements.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter, but the range is given as 'reasonable' rather than absolute — it is a starting point to adjust per typeface.

claim: Leave letter-spacing at the default for body copy and small UI text.
why: Design tools ship spacing metrics tuned for reading sizes, so manual adjustment there fixes nothing and risks harming legibility.
when: Paragraphs, labels, captions, and anything at typical interface sizes.

claim: Express letter-spacing as a percentage of font size rather than a fixed pixel value.
why: A percentage scales with the type, so one value keeps its optical effect across a responsive size ramp; a fixed pixel offset would over-tighten small text and under-tighten large text.
when: Defining tracking tokens in a type scale or design system.

claim: When a typeface that reads well in paragraphs looks loose or disjointed scaled up, treat it as a tracking problem before rejecting the font.
why: The defect is in the default spacing metrics at that size, not in the letterforms — swapping fonts wastes time and rarely fixes it.
when: Evaluating a typeface for a display or hero role.
fails: Some genuinely poor typefaces do break down at large sizes; tracking is the first fix to try, not a guaranteed one.

claim: Verify tracking changes by comparing tuned and untuned copies side by side rather than judging a single version.
why: The effect is subtle enough that it is hard to see in isolation, but obvious in direct comparison.
when: Dialing in any small optical typographic adjustment.
